title: john
description: John the Ripper (JtR) is an offline password cracker supporting hundreds of hash and cipher formats, with helper scripts to extract hashes from encrypted files (zip, PDF, SSH keys, and more).

Getting Started.Getting Started:
The community-maintained **"jumbo"** build is what almost everyone actually wants — the stock `john` core supports only about a dozen formats, while jumbo adds 470+. Current stable jumbo is **1.9.0-jumbo-1**; a rolling `bleeding-jumbo` development branch tracks ongoing work between releases.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S john
```

The Arch `extra` package builds the jumbo variant, so `john`, `zip2john`, `ssh2john`, `pdf2john`, and friends are all present after install.

## 2. Check the build

```bash
john --list=build-info
```

Confirms which optional features (OpenMP, GPU/OpenCL support via `--format=*-opencl`, etc.) your build includes.

## 3. First crack

```bash
unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > /tmp/combined.txt
john /tmp/combined.txt
```

Only meaningful against your own machine's hashes for a local audit — never run this against a shadow file you don't own. See [Legal Notes](/john/legal-notes/).
Getting Started.Cracking Modes:
John tries several modes in order by default; understanding them lets you target the right one instead of waiting through all of them.

## Single crack mode

```bash
john --single hashes.txt
```

Uses info from the hash file itself (usernames, GECOS fields) as candidate passwords with light mangling. Fast, and often the first hit for accounts using username-derived passwords.

## Wordlist mode

```bash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules hashes.txt
```

`--rules` applies mangling rules (leet-speak substitutions, appended digits, capitalization variants) to every wordlist entry, massively expanding effective coverage without a bigger wordlist.

## Incremental (brute-force) mode

```bash
john --incremental hashes.txt
```

Tries all character combinations in an optimized order based on character frequency statistics. Only practical for short hashes or fast hash types — this is where GPU offload to Hashcat usually makes more sense for anything non-trivial.

## Showing cracked results

```bash
john --show hashes.txt
```
Getting Started.Extracting Hashes:
Jumbo ships dozens of `*2john` helper scripts that pull a crackable hash out of a protected file format.

## Common ones

| Script | Extracts from |
| --- | --- |
| `zip2john` | ZIP archives (classic + AES) |
| `rar2john` | RAR archives |
| `pdf2john` | Password-protected PDFs |
| `ssh2john` | Encrypted OpenSSH private keys |
| `keepass2john` | KeePass `.kdbx` databases |
| `office2john` | Office `.docx`/`.xlsx`/`.pptx` |

## Workflow

```bash
ssh2john id_rsa > id_rsa.hash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt id_rsa.hash
john --show id_rsa.hash
```

This is also the standard hand-off point to Hashcat: extract with the `*2john` script, then feed the resulting hash line to `hashcat` if you want GPU-accelerated cracking instead — see the `hashcat` docs' [Attack Modes](/hashcat/attack-modes/) page.
Getting Started.Hash Formats And Detection:
John needs to know what *kind* of hash it's looking at before it can crack it — a raw MD5 hash and a bcrypt hash need completely different (and wildly different-cost) attack loops.

## Auto-detection

```bash
john hashes.txt
```

With no `--format`, John inspects each line's structure (length, prefix like `$6$` for sha512crypt, `$y$`/`$2b$` for bcrypt/yescrypt, etc.) and guesses. It usually gets this right for well-known formats, but ambiguous or malformed lines get skipped with a warning.

## Listing and forcing formats

```bash
john --list=formats
john --list=formats | grep -i sha
john --format=Raw-MD5 hashes.txt
```

`--list=formats` prints every format this build supports (jumbo ships 470+). Force one with `--format=NAME` whenever auto-detection guesses wrong, is ambiguous, or you know exactly what you extracted (e.g. straight after `zip2john`, the tool prints which `--format` to use in its own output).

## Benchmarking your hardware

```bash
john --test
john --test --format=bcrypt
```

`--test` runs a timed benchmark of one or all formats, reporting guesses/second. Worth running once after install: it's the fastest way to see just how much slower a deliberately slow format (bcrypt, sha512crypt, Argon2) is than a fast one (raw MD5/SHA1, NTLM) on your CPU — often several orders of magnitude, which is exactly why slow formats exist as a defense.

## The pot file

```bash
john --pot=myrun.pot --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt
```

Every cracked password is written to a "pot file" (`~/.john/john.pot` by default) so a hash is never attacked twice for nothing — rerunning the same job skips anything already in the pot and jumps straight to `--show`-able results. `--pot=<file>` points at a different one, handy for keeping separate engagements/audits from mixing results.

Guides.Custom Rules:
Rules transform each wordlist candidate before it's tried, dramatically increasing hit rate against human-chosen passwords.

## Using a built-in rule set

```bash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules=Jumbo hashes.txt
```

`--rules=Jumbo` is the large bundled rule set; `--rules` alone uses the smaller default `Single` rules section.

## Writing a custom rule

Add a section to `~/.john/john.local.conf`:

```ini
[List.Rules:Custom]
c $[0-9] $[0-9]
l c $!
u $2 $0 $2 $6
```

Each line is one transformation: `c` capitalizes, `$X` appends `X`, `l` lowercases the whole word. Run with:

```bash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules=Custom hashes.txt
```

## Combining wordlist + mask

```bash
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules --mask='^1?w?d?d' hashes.txt
```

Prepends `1` and appends two digits to every mangled wordlist candidate — useful for policies that force a digit and a leading/trailing character.

*Part of the [Extracting Hashes](/john/extracting-hashes/) page.* End-to-end script: extract a hash from a ZIP, crack it, print the result.

Source: `example/crack_zip.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ZIP="${1:?usage: crack_zip.sh <file.zip>}"

zip2john "$ZIP" > /tmp/zip.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt /tmp/zip.hash
john --show /tmp/zip.hash
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/crack_zip.sh
./example/crack_zip.sh secrets.zip
```
Guides.Mask Mode In Depth:
Mask mode generates candidates from a template of placeholders instead of a wordlist — the tool of choice when you know the *shape* of a password (a company's old policy, a partial memory of your own forgotten password) but not the exact value.

## Placeholder classes

| Placeholder | Expands to |
| --- | --- |
| `?l` | lowercase a-z |
| `?u` | uppercase A-Z |
| `?d` | digit 0-9 |
| `?s` | special characters |
| `?a` | all printable ASCII |
| `?b` | all 256 byte values |

```bash
john --mask='?u?l?l?l?l?d?d' hashes.txt
```

Matches "one capital, four lowercase letters, two digits" — e.g. `Pluto42`, a common human pattern.

## Custom character sets

```bash
john --mask='?1?1?1?1?d?d?d' -1='?l?u' hashes.txt
```

`-1` (and `-2`, `-3`...) defines a custom placeholder class; here `?1` means "either case of one letter," used four times before three digits.

## Ranges and known-partial passwords

```bash
john --mask='Summer20?d?d!' hashes.txt
```

Literal characters can sit right alongside placeholders — this tries `Summer2000!` through `Summer2099!`. This is the single most effective technique when you (or a user you're auditing with permission) remember the general pattern of a lost password but not the exact digits.

## Combining with a wordlist

```bash
john --wordlist=names.txt --mask='?w?d?d?s' hashes.txt
```

`?w` inserts the current wordlist word — so mask mode becomes "wordlist word, plus two digits, plus a symbol," covering the extremely common human habit of `Name99!`-style passwords far faster than incremental brute force.
Guides.Sessions, Resuming, And Status:
Cracking runs can take hours or days; John is built to be interrupted and resumed without losing progress.

## Naming a session

```bash
john --session=audit1 --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules hashes.txt
```

`--session=NAME` names the run, writing periodic state to `NAME.rec` so it can be restored later — always name long-running jobs rather than relying on the unnamed default session.

## Checking on a running job

Press a key (any key) in the terminal running John, and it prints a status line: elapsed time, guesses tried, current candidate rate, and an ETA for the current mode.

From another terminal:

```bash
john --status=audit1
```

## Interrupting and resuming

`Ctrl+C` stops a session cleanly and writes final state. Resume exactly where it left off:

```bash
john --restore=audit1
```

## Running across multiple machines/cores

```bash
# machine A
john --node=1/4 --fork=4 --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt
# machine B
john --node=2/4 --fork=4 --wordlist=rockyou.txt hashes.txt
```

`--node=K/N` splits the candidate space into `N` slices and processes slice `K` — combine with `--fork` for per-machine CPU parallelism, so a large wordlist+rules job can be spread across several machines without duplicating work.

CLI Reference.john:
## Synopsis

```
john [options] [password-files]
```

## Cracking modes

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--single[=SECTION]` | Single crack mode (uses hash-file metadata as candidates) |
| `--wordlist=FILE`, `-w=FILE` | Wordlist mode using `FILE` (`-` for stdin) |
| `--rules[=NAME]` | Apply mangling rules (default or a named `.conf` section) |
| `--incremental[=MODE]` | Brute-force mode using a named charset definition |
| `--mask=MASK` | Mask mode, e.g. `?u?l?l?l?d?d` |
| `--markov[=OPTIONS]` | Markov-chain mode, weighting guesses by statistical likelihood |
| `--external=NAME` | Use a custom cracking mode written in John's built-in scripting language |
| `--loopback[=FILE]` | Re-run using previously cracked passwords (default: the pot file) as the wordlist |
| `--stdin` | Read candidate passwords from stdin (for piping in another tool's output) |
| `--pipe` | Like `--stdin` but buffered for higher throughput |
| `--stdout[=LENGTH]` | Print generated candidates instead of testing them (for feeding other tools, e.g. Hashcat) |

## Targeting and format

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--format=NAME` | Force a specific hash/cipher format |
| `--list=formats` | List every supported format |
| `--list=build-info` | Show optional features this build was compiled with |
| `--list=subformats` | List subformats for formats that have them (e.g. dynamic hashes) |
| `--test[=TIME]` | Benchmark one or all formats |
| `--users=[-]LOGIN\|UID` | Restrict (or exclude, with `-`) to specific users |
| `--groups=[-]GID` | Restrict to specific groups (for `/etc/passwd`-style input) |
| `--shells=[-]SHELL` | Restrict by login shell |
| `--salts=[-]N` | Only attack salts shared by at least `N` hashes (efficiency for large dumps) |

## Length and charset constraints

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--min-length=N` | Skip candidates shorter than `N` |
| `--max-length=N` | Skip candidates longer than `N` |
| `--min-run=N` / `--max-run=N` | Bound repeated-character runs (rule/mask tuning) |
| `--encoding=NAME` | Candidate encoding (e.g. `UTF-8`) |
| `--input-encoding=NAME` | Encoding of the input hash file |
| `--target-encoding=NAME` | Encoding the target system used |

## Session control

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--session=NAME` | Name this run for later `--status`/`--restore` |
| `--restore[=NAME]` | Resume a named interrupted session |
| `--status[=NAME]` | Print status of a named session without resuming it |
| `--fork=N` | Fork `N` processes for CPU parallelism |
| `--node=MIN[-MAX]/TOTAL` | Process only this slice of the candidate space, for multi-machine runs |
| `--dupe-suppression` | Skip duplicate candidates a rule set might generate twice |
| `--skip-self-tests` | Skip the startup self-test (slightly faster launch) |

## Results

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--show[=left]` | Show cracked passwords for a hash file (`=left` shows only *un*cracked ones) |
| `--pot=FILE` | Use an alternate pot file instead of `~/.john/john.pot` |
| `--make-charset=FILE` | Build a custom charset file from a wordlist, for `--incremental` |

## GPU/OpenCL (jumbo)

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--format=NAME-opencl` | Use the OpenCL-accelerated variant of a format, where available |
| `--devices=LIST` | Select which OpenCL device(s) to use |
| `--list=opencl-devices` | List detected OpenCL devices |

Full manual: `man john` (jumbo build) or the `doc/` directory bundled with the source.

Project.FAQ:
### `No password hashes loaded`

John couldn't auto-detect the format of the input, or every hash in the file is a format John doesn't support. Try forcing detection with `--format=` and a guess (`--list=formats` shows all options), or confirm the `*2john` extraction script actually produced valid output.

### Cracking is much slower than Hashcat for the same hash

Expected for GPU-friendly hash types (fast hashes like raw MD5/SHA1, NTLM). John is primarily CPU-based; Hashcat's GPU backends are typically orders of magnitude faster for those formats. John still wins for many "unusual" formats and file-based extractions Hashcat doesn't cover as completely (some legacy Unix crypt variants, certain archive formats).

### `--fork` vs OpenMP — which should I use?

Use `--fork=N` for hash formats without OpenMP support, or when you want hard process isolation. For OpenMP-enabled formats, John already threads automatically based on `OMP_NUM_THREADS` — check `--list=build-info` to see if your build has OpenMP.

### Which mode should I actually try first?

Roughly in this order of cost-to-benefit: `--single` (seconds, often free hits), a good wordlist with `--rules` (minutes to hours, catches most human passwords), `--mask` if you know or suspect the password's shape, and `--incremental` only as a last resort for short/fast hashes since it's the slowest per-hit method.

### How do I know a crack actually finished/failed?

John prints `Session completed` when it exhausts the current mode. Nothing found doesn't mean "impossible" — it means this specific mode/wordlist/mask didn't contain the password; try a bigger wordlist, add `--rules`, or narrow a mask based on any policy hints you have.

### Can I feed John's candidates into Hashcat instead?

Yes — `john --stdout --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rules | hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt` pipes John's mangling engine into Hashcat's GPU cracking loop, combining John's rich rule syntax with Hashcat's speed. See the [hashcat docs](/hashcat/) for the `-m` mode numbers.

Project.Legal Notes:
John the Ripper (and every `*2john` extraction script) is a standard, legitimate tool for **auditing password strength on systems and files you own or are explicitly authorized to test** — security teams use it to find weak credentials before an attacker does, and it's part of most professional pentesting and CTF curricula.

Running it against hashes, accounts, or encrypted files you don't own or don't have explicit written authorization to test is unauthorized access in most jurisdictions, independent of whether the crack succeeds. In practice that means:

- Cracking your own `/etc/shadow` on a box you administer: fine.
- Cracking a client's hashes as part of a signed penetration-testing engagement: fine, scoped to the engagement.
- Cracking a password-protected ZIP/PDF/document you created and forgot the password to: fine.
- Cracking hashes, archives, or accounts belonging to someone else without their permission: not fine, regardless of intent.

If you're learning, practice against your own test files and hashes, or purpose-built legal targets (CTF platforms, hash-cracking practice sets explicitly published for that purpose).

Learn by Examples.Auditing A Team's Password Hygiene:
A small team wants to know, before an attacker does, whether any of their Linux server accounts or an old encrypted backup archive use weak passwords. This walkthrough is written for that authorized, on-your-own-infrastructure scenario (see [Legal Notes](/john/legal-notes/)) and touches most of what John can do.

## 1. Confirm the build and benchmark the hardware

```bash
john --list=build-info
john --test
```

`--test` gives a feel for guesses/second on this machine — useful context for later deciding how big a wordlist or mask job is realistic before the audit window closes.

## 2. Extract crackable hashes from the system

```bash
sudo unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > /tmp/combined.txt
```

`unshadow` merges the two files into the single-file format John expects, since `/etc/shadow`'s hashes alone don't carry the usernames John's `--single` mode wants.

## 3. First pass: single crack mode (fast, free hits)

```bash
john --single --format=sha512crypt /tmp/combined.txt
```

Catches anyone using their own username or GECOS info (real name, etc.) as a password — often finds one or two accounts in seconds with zero configuration.

## 4. Second pass: wordlist plus rules

```bash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules=Jumbo \
  --format=sha512crypt /tmp/combined.txt
```

`--rules=Jumbo` mangles every wordlist entry (capitalization, appended digits, leet-speak) — this is where most real-world weak passwords fall.

## 5. Check progress without stopping the job

Leave it running in one terminal; from another:

```bash
john --status
```

Or press a key in the running terminal for a live status line with an ETA.

## 6. Targeted mask for a known password policy

Say the team's old password policy required "Capital letter, 5-7 lowercase letters, 2 digits." Rather than waiting on incremental brute force:

```bash
john --mask='?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d' --format=sha512crypt /tmp/combined.txt
```

## 7. See what's been cracked so far

```bash
john --show /tmp/combined.txt
```

Prints `username:password` for every hash cracked across *all* the runs above — John never re-attacks a hash already solved in the pot file, so each pass above only spent time on what remained.

## 8. Now check that old encrypted backup archive

```bash
zip2john old-backup.zip > /tmp/zip.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --rules /tmp/zip.hash
john --show /tmp/zip.hash
```

## 9. Name and checkpoint a long final run

Overnight, throw a bigger job at whatever's left:

```bash
john --session=overnight --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  --rules=Jumbo --format=sha512crypt --users=-root /tmp/combined.txt
```

`--session=overnight` means it can be safely interrupted (`Ctrl+C`) and resumed tomorrow with `john --restore=overnight`; `--users=-root` skips the root account, which should be locked down separately (e.g. key-only login) rather than password-audited at all.

## What this walkthrough covered

`unshadow`, `zip2john`, `--single`, `--wordlist`, `--rules`, `--mask` placeholders, `--format`, `--status`, `--show`, the pot file's automatic dedup, `--session`/`--restore`, and `--users` filtering — the full day-to-day loop of a legitimate password audit.
